annotations.text:
The layout problem

Twenty rows, nineteen of them entirely empty — six columns of "—" and "No jobs-page salary".

A dense comparison table is the right instrument for comparing many companies, and the wrong one for saying that one has a figure and nineteen do not.

The top is three cold metrics and a line of methodology, so nothing says in words what you are looking at — and nothing says why the company in the card is the one in the card.

A podium, then the page reads downward

Overview's palette in a different shape — a band, not a grid of tiles.

The band leads with the podium rather than one company, so "why this one" is visible instead of asserted: it is first on whatever the page is ranked by, and the two behind it are named with the gap. The filters under the band decide it — change the level, the location or what it is ranked on and the podium reorders.

Six of the leader's own numbers carry the detail. Compare's band diverges deliberately: there, each measure shows its own leader and position.

The table holds only companies that have a figure; the rest become one calm block that says why.
